text: We moved our background jobs off cron and onto a queue last quarter. The migration took three weeks longer than estimated, mostly because of retry semantics we had not thought through. Worth it in the end.

There is a common misconception that adding more caching layers always improves performance. In practice, each layer adds a place where data can go stale, and debugging staleness costs more engineering time than the latency ever did.

I spent the weekend reading through the source of a library we depend on. It was a useful exercise. Most of the behavior I considered surprising turned out to be documented, just not in the place I was looking.
Our error rate dropped by roughly forty percent after we added request timeouts. The lesson is not that timeouts are magic. It is that unbounded waits turn one slow dependency into a full outage.

When onboarding new engineers, we now pair them with someone for the first two weeks instead of handing over a document. Documentation goes out of date. A person answering questions in real time does not.
The hardest part of distributed systems is not the algorithms. It is that failure modes compose in ways nobody anticipated, and your monitoring only covers the ones you already thought of.
We ran an experiment comparing two ranking models over four weeks. The newer model won on offline metrics and lost on engagement. We shipped the older one and wrote down why.
Type systems do not eliminate bugs. They eliminate a category of bugs and shift your attention to the remaining ones. That trade is usually worth making, but it should be described honestly.
A short note on code review: the goal is shared understanding, not gatekeeping. If a review thread runs past ten comments, move it to a call. Text is a poor medium for disagreement.
We deleted about eight thousand lines of code this month. None of it was broken. All of it supported a feature that three customers used and none of them missed.
Benchmarks in isolation are misleading. A function that is twice as fast in a microbenchmark may be slower in production because it no longer fits in cache alongside everything else running.
The team adopted trunk based development six months ago. Merge conflicts went down, and so did the average size of a change. The second effect mattered more than the first.
I used to believe that good architecture was about picking the right abstractions up front. Now I think it is mostly about making it cheap to change your mind later.
Rate limiting is easy to implement and hard to tune. Set it too low and you break legitimate clients. Set it too high and it does nothing during the incident you built it for.
Our postmortems used to assign blame implicitly through phrasing. We changed the template to describe systems rather than people, and participation in writing them went up noticeably.
Feature flags accumulate. We now require an expiry date on every flag at creation time, and a weekly job opens a ticket for the expired ones. It is bureaucratic and it works.
Reading the database query log for an hour taught me more about our application than a week of reading application code. The queries show what the system actually does under load.
There is a tendency to reach for a message broker whenever two services need to communicate. Often a synchronous call with a sensible timeout is simpler and easier to reason about.
We measured how long it takes a new hire to ship their first change to production. Reducing that number from eleven days to two required no new tooling, only removing approval steps.
Machine learning models degrade quietly. Unlike a service that returns errors, a stale model keeps returning confident predictions that are increasingly wrong. Monitoring has to be built for that.
The most useful refactor we did last year was giving every background task a name that appears in logs. It sounds trivial. It cut incident diagnosis time roughly in half.
Estimation improves when you estimate ranges instead of points. A task that takes between two and nine days is a different planning object than one that takes five.
I have come to prefer boring technology for infrastructure and interesting technology for products. The failure modes of boring systems are documented by people who already hit them.
Every configuration option is a promise to support that combination forever. We audited ours and found that eleven of thirty options had never been changed from their defaults by any customer.
Latency percentiles matter more than averages. The average request time can improve while the experience gets worse for the users who were already having the worst time.
We started writing a design document before any project over two weeks. Half the value comes from the writing itself, which surfaces disagreements that would otherwise appear in code review.
Automated tests are a form of documentation that cannot go stale silently. When a test breaks, someone has to decide whether the behavior or the expectation was wrong.
The migration is technically complete but operationally unfinished. Both systems still run, and the old one still receives traffic from two internal tools nobody has claimed ownership of.
